vignette:
He is forty-eight now, a Middle Eastern man who has spent most of his adult life working with fabric, shape, and color, and he still describes himself first as a fashion designer before anything else. For years, his life is organized around seasonal deadlines, fittings, garment racks, late nights in the studio, and the private satisfaction of turning an idea into something people want to wear. He likes precision. He notices hems that are half a centimeter off, the pull of a seam across the shoulder, the way a certain shade changes under different light. Before the disaster, he experiences this sensitivity as a gift, part of what makes him good at his work.

The event happens on an ordinary workday in a commercial building where he is meeting suppliers and reviewing materials for an upcoming collection. He remembers the fluorescent lighting, the hum of air conditioning, bolts of cloth stacked against a wall. Then there is a violent explosion. At first his mind cannot make sense of it. He thinks something heavy has fallen from above, but the sound keeps expanding in his body before he understands it with words. The building shudders. Glass bursts inward. Smoke and dust erase the room. Someone nearby screams in a high, animal sound he says he still hears sometimes when he is trying to fall asleep.

He drops to the floor without deciding to. There is blood on another man’s face, gray dust on his own hands, the smell of burning plastic and concrete. He crawls because he cannot see well enough to stand. In those minutes, he is certain he will die. He thinks of his children, though they are already nearly grown, and then feels ashamed later that his next thought is absurdly practical: that he has not sent final sketches to a client. When he finally reaches a stairwell and is pushed along by the crowd, he feels both frozen and frantic, moving because others are moving. Outside, sirens layer over one another. People are running, some filming, some shouting names. He cannot stop staring at the broken windows above, expecting another blast.

In the first weeks after, he tells himself he is lucky. He is alive. He has no major physical injuries beyond cuts and bruises. Friends call him resilient. He repeats the story too clearly, almost like he is narrating something that happened to someone else. He returns to work quickly because deadlines do not pause for catastrophe, and because the studio feels like the one place where his hands know what to do. But he finds that they tremble when a delivery cart slams into a wall. If a steam press hisses too loudly, his heart kicks hard in his chest. He starts scanning every room for exits before he notices the clothing or the people in it.

His work begins to change in ways he does not mention at first. He avoids going into tall commercial buildings unless he has no choice. He asks assistants to handle supplier meetings. He becomes irritated when interns leave boxes in the walkway, telling them sharply that they are creating hazards. During fittings, if several people talk at once, he loses track of what is being said. He starts forgetting appointments, then overcompensates by checking his calendar obsessively. At night he sleeps in fragments. He wakes drenched in sweat, convinced for a few seconds that the ceiling is coming down. Some mornings he sits on the edge of the bed and does not want to move, already exhausted by the idea of the day.

He is divorced, and although he and his ex-wife manage a workable relationship around their children, he becomes more withdrawn from both family and friends after the explosion. When his daughter asks why he no longer comes to crowded restaurants, he tells her he is tired of noise. It is partly true. Noise feels dangerous now. He avoids news coverage of attacks and disasters, but images still find him. A generator backfiring in the street makes him duck instinctively. Once, during a fashion show, a lighting malfunction causes a sharp popping sound backstage, and he has to lock himself in a restroom stall, breathing through panic and shame while models and assistants look for him.

He does not think of himself as frightened so much as changed. He says he has become “harder” and “smaller” at the same time. He used to enjoy wandering crowded markets for inspiration, touching trims and old textiles, bargaining over coffee. Now he prefers ordering materials online, even though he distrusts buying fabric without feeling it first. He keeps his studio immaculate, pathways clear, emergency numbers posted, batteries checked. He knows these habits are excessive, but they also soothe him.

Months become years, and from the outside his life appears intact. He continues producing collections. Clients still respect his eye. But his world is organized more and more around prevention and control. He sits with his back to walls. He startles easily. He ruminates about the people who died that day, especially a younger worker he saw injured on the floor and could not help. He wonders whether he should have done more, moved faster, stayed longer. He speaks about this quietly, looking down at his hands, as if he is still seeing the dust on them. Even now, in safe rooms, some part of him remains braced for the next blast.
